discovery: The cavity method and message-passing theory of random constraint-satisfaction problems, revealing glassy phase transitions in computation
motivation: Mézard and Zecchina turned the physics of spin glasses into a predictive science of complex systems far beyond magnetism. Mézard developed the cavity method, a physically transparent reformulation of replica symmetry breaking that can be applied to single instances on sparse random graphs. Together, they used it to compute exactly the satisfiability threshold of random K-SAT, discovered the clustering (dynamical) transition where solutions shatter into exponentially many glassy states, and from this physical insight invented survey propagation, an algorithm solving problems far beyond previous reach. Their work showed that phase transitions and broken ergodicity govern the hardness of computation, and it founded a vigorous field linking statistical physics with computer science, information theory, inference and machine learning. Many of these predictions were later proven rigorously by mathematicians. It is a beautiful example of a simple-looking problem, hard to understand, illuminated by deep physical ideas.
